faq.a: Yes; the risk is higher for non‑homogeneous lesions and for those with severe dysplasia on biopsy.
Biopsy is recommended for any lesion that is non‑homogeneous, larger than 2 cm, or shows suspicious change; if unavailable, arrange referral.
Cessation may lead to partial regression, especially for homogeneous lesions, but surveillance is still needed.

exam: What clinical features differentiate oral leukoplakia from oral candidiasis? — Non‑scrapable white plaque versus scrapable curd‑like lesions; candidiasis often erythematous underneath.

A 55‑year‑old smoker presents with a 1 cm homogeneous white patch on the buccal mucosa. What is your next step? — Perform gentle scraping; if non‑scrapable, arrange incisional biopsy to assess dysplasia.
Why is a non‑homogeneous (speckled) leukoplakia considered higher risk? — Presence of red areas indicates possible dysplasia or carcinoma in situ, raising malignant potential.

In a low‑resource hospital without pathology services, how would you manage a suspicious oral leukoplakia? — Counsel on risk‑factor cessation, perform oral brush cytology if possible, and refer urgently to a centre with biopsy capability.

Which systemic condition is most associated with oral hairy leukoplakia, and how does it differ from classic leukoplakia? — HIV infection; lesions are corrugated, lateral tongue, EBV‑related, and usually scrapable.
What red‑flag symptom in a patient with known leukoplakia warrants urgent referral? — New ulceration, rapid growth, bleeding, or pain.

Explain why laser ablation may be preferred over surgical excision for a small, non‑homogeneous lesion in a resource‑limited setting. — It provides precise removal with minimal tissue loss, can be done under local anaesthesia, and reduces postoperative morbidity.
How does betel quid chewing contribute to oral leukoplakia? — The areca nut and added tobacco act as chronic irritants and carcinogens, increasing plaque formation and dysplasia risk.
ai.title: Oral Leukoplakia
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Oral leukoplakia is a white, non‑scrapable plaque of the oral mucosa that may harbour dysplasia and progress to cancer. Diagnosis relies on exclusion of other causes and, when possible, biopsy. Management focuses on risk‑factor removal, surveillance and treatment of dysplasia.

b: Excludes candidiasis, lichen planus, trauma, and oral hairy leukoplakia.
Biopsy is gold standard for dysplasia grading; if unavailable, refer for specialist review.
sections.p: A clinical diagnosis of a white patch of oral mucosa that cannot be rubbed off and cannot be explained by another condition. Must be confirmed by history, examination and, if available, biopsy to assess dysplasia.

b: Homogeneous: flat, uniformly white – lower malignant potential.
Non‑homogeneous (speckled, verrucous): higher risk of severe dysplasia or carcinoma.
sections.p: Severity is graded histologically (WHO dysplasia grades: mild, moderate, severe, carcinoma in situ). Clinically, lesions are described by size, location and whether they are homogeneous or non‑homogeneous.

b: Tobacco smoking and smokeless tobacco (chewing, snuff).
Alcohol excess – synergistic with tobacco.
Chronic mechanical irritation (sharp teeth, ill‑fitting dentures).
Betel quid chewing (common in East Africa coastal communities).
HIV infection – may present as oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV).
Use of herbal or traditional remedies causing mucosal irritation.
sections.p: Most oral leukoplakia is linked to chronic irritants and carcinogens, especially tobacco use. In low‑resource settings, additional contributors are common infections and traditional practices.

b: White, well‑demarcated, non‑scrapable plaque.
Often >5 mm; larger lesions carry higher risk.
May be solitary or multiple.
sections.p: Patients notice a persistent white patch that does not disappear with scraping. It may be asymptomatic or cause mild irritation. Lesions are most frequent on the buccal mucosa, lateral tongue, and floor of mouth.
Investigations aim to confirm diagnosis, grade dysplasia and identify risk factors.

t.b: Distinguish leukoplakia from scrapable lesions (candidiasis). A non‑scrapable plaque supports leukoplakia.
Determines presence and grade of dysplasia. If unavailable, arrange referral to a centre with pathology services.
Quantifies exposure; guides counseling and risk stratification.

t.a: HIV rapid test (if risk factors present)
t.b: Detects underlying immunosuppression that may alter management.

t.a: Oral brush cytology (where biopsy not feasible)
t.b: Provides cellular atypia information; less sensitive than biopsy but useful when pathology is inaccessible.

b: Rapid increase in size or change in texture.
Development of ulceration, induration, or bleeding.
Non‑homogeneous appearance (speckled, verrucous).
Persistent pain or dysphagia.
sections.p: Key warning signs that suggest malignant transformation or urgent need for intervention.

b: Cessation of tobacco and alcohol; provide brief counseling and nicotine replacement if available.
Removal of mechanical irritants – smooth sharp teeth, adjust dentures.
Topical retinoids (e.g., tretinoin) for mild dysplasia where surgery is not feasible; avoid in pregnancy.
Surgical excision or laser ablation for moderate‑to‑severe dysplasia or non‑homogeneous lesions.
Follow‑up biopsy if lesion recurs or changes.
sections.p: Treat the underlying irritant, monitor for dysplasia, and intervene when high‑risk features are present.

b: Review every 3–6 months for high‑risk lesions; every 12 months for low‑risk homogeneous lesions.
Educate on oral self‑examination.
Vaccination against HPV (where available) to lower future oral cancer risk.
Oral candidiasis – scrapable white plaques that resolve with antifungals.
Oral hairy leukoplakia – corrugated lateral tongue lesions in HIV, EBV‑related.
Lichen planus – white reticular lines (Wickham striae) often bilateral.
sections.p: Conditions that can mimic oral leukoplakia.

b: Negative biopsy does not rule out future dysplasia; repeat if lesion persists.
Brush cytology may miss focal severe dysplasia – treat as suspicious if clinical risk is high.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid growth, ulceration, bleeding, or new pain in a known leukoplakia lesion.
